Case No. 8

atoms.reference: Professional manuals, devices and techniques that promised to make writing easier or to automate it, on a timeline from circa 1890 to 1970: Wycliffe Hill's Plot Genies, William Wallace Cook's Plotto, the patents of Arthur Blanchard and Henrietta Rose Montague, plot generators with spinning devices, Christopher Strachey's love letter program, Margaret Masterman's machine translation, Georges Polti's thirty-six situations (1895), Harry Stephen Keeler's web-word designs.

evidence.record_quote: Following a timeline from circa 1890–1970, this exhibition explores professional manuals, devices, and techniques that promised to make writing easier—and even to automate it.
such as Wycliffe Hill’s Plot Genies, and plot generators such as William Wallace Cook’s Plotto series.
Automated text generation catalyzed a wave of early 20th-century patents, from Arthur Blanchard’s “movie-writer” machine and Henrietta Rose Montague’s “name selector.”
Some how-to manuals incorporated simple plot generators, with spinning devices or automatic number generators that would guide would-be novelists past writers’ block.
from Christopher Strachey, who wrote a love letter program in the 1940s, to Margaret Masterman, a linguist who pioneered the use of computers to aid automatic translation.
Georges Polti’s Les trente-six situations dramatiques (1895)
Harry Stephen Keeler’s “web-word” designs
